docs.text: The Aether: Spatial Behavior Software Suite, is a set of tools and interfaces for designing the behavior of active and responsive environments. Aether also provides tools to facilitate the long-term operation of these spaces. Use Cases. ¶ Developed by the Living Architecture Systems Group and Philip Beesley Studio Inc. Aether was originally created to support Living Architecture Testbeds, and its design has been informed by many years of testing and evolution in the control systems of these deeply immersive environments. Key Concepts. ¶ Distributed Topology: ¶ Entities in Aether are designed for distributed computation. This allows the system to be scalable (new devices add minimal computational overhead to the central server), and robust (entities are resilient to network disruption and can continue basic operation without a connection to the server) Spatial Behavior: ¶ Entities in Aether exist in 3D space, and their spatial relationships to their environment and other entities inform their behavior. Thin Shell Interface: ¶ Aether is designed as a Thin Shell , a co-ordinating interface that can speak to many different kinds of hardware and software using open protocols (generally OSC)

docs.text: Home ¶ Introduction ¶ The Aether software suite establishes and maintains the behaviour system for Living Architecture Testbeds. It consists of four components which operate together to enable persistent, coordinated and controllable behaviour within the testbed: Microcontroller firmware (C++) within each ESP-32 Node Controller (NC) device within the system establishes a distributed means for elements to respond to influences A Node.js server (Javascript) to coordinate the distributed elements within the system and serve the browser-based control pages Browser-based software (Javascript) to create Graphical User Interface (GUI) elements for controlling behaviour logic and influences within the environment A realtime database (Firebase) to maintain the configuration of the system, its settings and its various user sessions and contexts Key functional principles used in the testbeds include Influence Engines : Layered, spatialized algorithms that establish influence on elements of the system Reactor Cells : Elements within a node-controller that respond to stimulus via coordinated time-based reaction profiles Subscription : Means by which specific node controllers become aware of and sensitive to influences Because the system is distributed among various platforms, code is reused wherever possible. To enable functional aspects of the browser-based GUI representations of node controllers, for example, some of the C++ code that the physical microcontrollers use is compiled into Web Assembly (WASM) modules that are integrated into the javascript running on these pages. Similarly, the core of each Influence Engine is implemented once in C++ and then used as a WASM within the browser to visualize the effect of the influence engines. docs.text: Setting up the Build System ¶ Note The following instructions document how to setup Zig and PlatformIO for a Standalone Aether Server running on a Raspberry Pi. Please see the Zig and PlatformIO documentation for install instructions for other operating systems. To modify Firmware for a node controller you will need Zig installed. To manage Zig version we will install ZVM. Run curl https://www.zvm.app/install.sh | bash Run source /home/aether/.bashrc to start using ZVM in the same terminal Run zvm install 0.15.2 to install the specific version of zig we need. Zig should now be installed. To test that firmware compilation is working switch to the firmware directory with cd firmware and run zig build (this will take several minutes). This command will recompile the Web Assembly Modules used for the Influence Engines and Logic Editor. To get the compilation system ready to build firmware for our Node Controller Devices, we also need to install PlatformIO. run the included python script to install Platform IO, python3 get-platformio.py add pio to the PATH. run sudo nano ~/.bashrc scroll to the bottom and add the line export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.platformio/penv/bin" use CTRL X to exit, Y to confirm changes and ENTER to complete the addition run source ~/.bashrc for these changes to take effect in this terminal Platform IO should now be installed, you can test its working by running zig build arduino for compile firmware for Node Controller devices You are now setup to edit Aether's Influence Engines and Logic Reactor Blocks and compile them to Web Assembly for the user interface, and to device firmware.

Creating a Logic Reactor Block. ¶ Creating a custom logic editor block allows you to add new functionality to logic graphs made with the logic editor. In this example, we'll create a block that implements both the OR and Exclusive OR logical operators. Creating a new logic block will involve editing the following files Adding the new block class in firmware/src/Blocks.h Adding our block to the block constructor in firmware/src/Blocks.cpp Creating a new module in server/public/logic/modules/[NEW BLOCK].js Updating the list of modules in server/public/logic/modules.js Adding a New Block to Blocks.h ¶ Block Class Structure ¶ We'll start by creating the functionality of the block in firmware/src/Blocks.h . Each block is defined as a class within this file, and each new block inherits from the parent Block class. A typical block class is structured like this: class [BlockName] : public Block { public: // declare inputs and their types float value = 0.0; // declare properties and their types. float property = 0.0; // declare outputs and their types. float outputA = 0.0; float outputB = 0.0; // Initialize our inputs and outputs virtual void init() { inputs.addInput("value", &value, {}, 0); inputs.addProperty("property", &property, {.min = 0, .max = 1, .step = 0.1}); outputs.add("outputA", &outputA, {}); outputs.add("outputB", &outputB, {}); } // define the logic that happens when our block runs virtual void execute(unsigned long millis) { //logic goes here } }; Variable Declaration ¶ For our OR block we'll be looking to create a block with 2 boolean inputs, a parameter that allows the user to set if this is an OR or an Exclusive OR, and a single output. We'll set up the block initially with the following: class OrBlock : public Block { public: // declare inputs and their types bool inputA = false; bool inputB = false; // declare properties and their types. bool exclusive = false; // declare outputs and their types. bool output = false; Initialization ¶ Once we've declared our inputs, parameters, and outputs, we need to initialize our block. Initializing adds our blocks and parameters to the Input and Output tables ( Tables are a internal data structure used throughout Aether to facilitate memory access and management within WASM's ). When we add parameters to the Table we can define some extra options that will determine how the User Interface is will be generated. Adding an input uses the addInput() method of the inputs table, which looks like: inputs.addInput("inputA", &inputA, {}, false); where: "inputA" is the String Name of our input &inputA is the memory address of our inputA variable declared above ( the & operator returns the memory address of a variable in c++ ) { } is the set of additional options declared for this input, for simple inputs this can typically be left empty false is the declared baseline for this input (what the input defaults to if nothing is connected) Adding a property uses the addProperty() of the inputs table which looks like: inputs.addProperty("property", &property, {.min = 0, .max = 1, .step = 0.1}); This is very similar to the addInput method, but Properties do not have a baseline value defined, and often make use of the additional options argument. Available options that can be defined for a property are: Type Property Description Default Value float .min The Minimum value for this property 0 float .max The Maximum value for this property 1.0 float .step The Step size to use for the UI slider ( smaller values give finer control ) 0.01 bool .display Should this property be displayed in the UI true char .unit Units to display for this value (mm, cm, m/s etc.) None Adding an output uses the add() method of the outputs table, which looks like: outputs.add("outputA", &outputA, {}); where: "outputA" is the String Name of our input &outputA is the memory address of our inputA variable declared above ( the & operator returns the memory address of a variable in c++ ) { } is the set of additional options declared for this input, for simple inputs this can typically be left empty Using these Methods we can construct the init() method of our new block. // Initialize our inputs and outputs virtual void init() { inputs.addInput("inputA", &inputA, {}, false); inputs.addInput("inputB", &inputB, {}, false); // We won't use any additional options here as our property is a boolean value inputs.addProperty("exclusive", &exclusive, {}); outputs.add("output", &output, {}); } Executing Logic ¶ With our inputs, properties and outputs initialized we can start writing the logic of our block. The execute function does not return a value, it sets the output variables declared above to the desired value based on the inputs and parameters. ( Note the execute function always receives a relative time in milliseconds as an argument, which can be useful for blocks dealing with time, however it is not used in this example ) The execute function for our or block looks like this: virtual void execute(unsigned long millis) { if (exclusive){ output = (inputA || inputB) && (inputA != inputB); } else{ output = inputA || inputB; } } The full class of our OrBlock block to be added to the Blocks.h file looks like: class OrBlock : public Block { public: // declare inputs and their types bool inputA = false; bool inputB = false; // declare properties and their types. bool exclusive = false; // declare outputs and their types. bool output = false; // Initialize our inputs and outputs virtual void init() { inputs.addInput("inputA", &inputA, {}, false); inputs.addInput("inputB", &inputB, {}, false); // We won't use any additional options here as our property is a boolean value inputs.addProperty("exclusive", &exclusive, {}); outputs.add("output", &output, {}); } // Execute our logic virtual void execute(unsigned long millis) { if (exclusive){ output = (inputA || inputB) && (inputA != inputB); } else{ output = inputA || inputB; } } }; Updating the Block Constructor in Blocks.cpp ¶ Now that we've created our block class, we need to add it to the Block constructor defined in firmware/src/Blocks.cpp . The block constructor starts around line 13 and begins with Block *newBlock(const char *type) { followed by a long list of conditional statements. To the end of this list of conditionals, we need to add the condition of our new block. We'll do this by adding another else if condition at the end of the list before the errorLog(" Can't find %s in Blocks.cpp .... ", type); warning. Our new condition will look like: else if (strcmp(type, "OrBlock") == 0){ return new OrBlock(); } This completes the creation of the block on the firmware side of the Aether Code base. Recompile WASM's and Firmware. ¶ With the firmware side complete we can rebuild the Web Assembly Modules from the firmware folder by running zig build in the terminal. We can also upload firmware with our new block to our devices via OTA or directly over usb. In the next section we'll create the files necessary to include our new block in the Logic Editor UI. Creating a new module ¶ To make our new block display in the User Interface of the Logic Reactor we need to create a new module that defines how the block will be drawn. This module will be added to server/public/logic/modules/ and should match the class name of the block defined in Blocks.h . for this example we'll create OrBlock.js and add it to the modules folder. The following template can be used to create a new block module: import { html } from "../../global.js" import { Position } from "../../libraries/xyflow.js" import { NodeContainer } from "../components.js" import { useErrorSignal } from "../../components/hooks.js"; import { millis } from "../shared.js" export const inputs = { } export const outputs = { } export function initWasm(data) { } export function execute({}, data) { data.wasm.executeBlock(millis()); } export function Display({data}) { return html` <${NodeContainer} data=${data}>
` } export function DisplayIcon() { return html` <${NodeContainer}>
` } The inputs and outputs constants need to be populated with the inputs and outputs of our block. Each input and output must be added as a Javascript Object, with the following properties: inputA: { type: "number", description: "First value", position: Position.Left, }, Property Description type The Javascript type of this input (*in general this should always be "number") desciription A description of this input position determines where the input will appear on the block. Options are Position.Left, Position.Right, Position.Top, Position.Bottom. Note we generally use Left or Top for inputs, with the outputs directly across from the input (Right or Bottom) Note The spelling of the input or output must match exactly with the String Name of the input or output that was defined in the initialization function of the block class. The complete input and output constants for our OR block would look like: export const inputs = { inputA: { type: "number", description: "First Value", position: Position.Left, }, inputB: { type: "number", description: "Second Value", position: Position.Left, }, } export const outputs = { output: { type: "number", description: "Result", position: Position.Right, }, } The Display() and DisplayIcon() functions allow us to describe how a block will look in the Logic Editor using Javascript and HTML. Replacing the Text in the template with text will create a simple text label for the block. In the Display() function we also have access to data about inputs, outputs and parameters of the block. In our example, we'll use this to change our simple text label depending on the 'exclusive' property of our block: export function Display({data}) { const exclusive_ref = useErrorSignal(data.data.settings, "exclusive") let label_text = "OR" if(exclusive_ref.value){label_text = "XOR"} return html` <${NodeContainer} data=${data}>
${label_text}
` } We use const exclusive_ref = useErrorSignal(data.data.settings, "exclusive") call to get a reference to the "exclusive" property of our block. We can check the value of this reference using exclusive_ref.value and use this to change the text that appears in the block label. The full code of our OrBlock.js file is: import { html } from "../../global.js" import { Position } from "../../libraries/xyflow.js" import { NodeContainer } from "../components.js" import { useErrorSignal } from "../../components/hooks.js"; import { millis } from "../shared.js" export const inputs = { inputA: { type: "number", description: "First Value", position: Position.Left, }, inputB: { type: "number", description: "Second Value", position: Position.Left, }, } export const outputs = { output: { type: "number", description: "Result", position: Position.Right, }, } export function initWasm(data) { } export function execute({}, data) { data.wasm.executeBlock(millis()); } export function Display({data}) { const exclusive_ref = useErrorSignal(data.data.settings, "exclusive") let label_text = "OR" if(exclusive_ref.value){label_text = "XOR"} return html` <${NodeContainer} data=${data}>
${label_text}
` } export function DisplayIcon() { return html` <${NodeContainer}>
OR
` } Updating Modules.js ¶ Finally we need to update the server/public/logic/modules.js file to include our new module. Open the file and add the following to the imports at the top of the file: import * as OrBlock from "./modules/OrBlock.js"; We also need to add our imported OrBlock to the export const modules = { list below. Once this has been added our new Logic Block is complete!

docs.text: Editing Aether ¶ Introduction ¶ For more advanced use, users may want to access and edit Aether's source code, to create new Influence Engines , or new Logic Reactor Blocks . With Raspberry Pi Image ¶ Connect to the Raspberry Pi with VSCode Remote (using the same password as SSH) Open the testbed-v4 folder Open a terminal. Building WASM's and Firmware ¶ Note If you are using the latest Rapsberry Pi Image, your Pi should already have the necessary libraries and tools installed to build Aethers firmware and WASM's. If Zig and PlatformIO are not installed on your system see the guide on setting up the build system Building Web Assembly Modules (WASM's) ¶ Aether uses Web Assembly Modules to share code between the device firmware and web interface. To compile the Web Assembly Modules for the web interface: move to the firmware directory with cd firmware run zig build This will compile the Web Assembly Modules and move them to their correct locations for the web interface to use them. Building Firmware for Devices ¶ Running zig build arduino will compile firmware binaries for all supported device types. Over the Air Firmware Updates ¶ If a device is already connected to Aether, you can use the Over the Air (OTA) update system in the Aether Dashboard. Select the device you'd like to update, and press the "OTA Firmware Update" button in the Hardware -> Troubleshooting Tools panel of the dashboard. This will send the last firmware compiled on the Raspberry Pi to this device. Directly Connected Firmware Update, ¶ For Devices that are not connected to Aether, you can compile firmware directly to the device. Connect the device to the Raspberry Pi using a micro usb cable. Ensure your remote terminal is in the firmware folder run pio run -e featheresp32 --target upload This will compile the firmware and upload it to the device.

docs.text: Creating an Influence Engine ¶ Warning This documentation page is a work in progress and is not complete. Introduction to Influence Engines ¶ Influence Engines are Algorithms At the heart of LASG’s behaviour system is the concept of Influence Engines. An influence engine is a piece of software that algorithmically generates ‘influences’ on the various spatially distributed parts of the sculpture. For example, a simple influence engine might create waveforms that move through the sculpture by determining the amplitude of a wave at various physical locations in the space. A different Influence Engine might use particle dynamics to calculate the trajectory of virtual objects which influence elements within the sculpture. Overview ¶ An influence engine needs a name, for this guide the influence engine will be called Ambient Waves, and it will simply create an infinite moving sine wave of influence, with specific angle, period, amplitude and velocity (seen from plan view). This wave will exert an influence proportional to the amplitude of the sine wave in any given location (offset so that its influence is read from 0.0-1.0). Inputs, outputs, parameters and events Browser-based visualization and graphical interface Third-party tool integration (eg. Max MSP) Events ¶ Firmware ¶ Implement an influence Engine in CPP ¶ Copy ExampleEngine.h to AmbientWaves.h and rename all the instances of ExampleEngine to AmbientWaves. Copy ExampleEngine.cpp to AmbientWaves.cpp and rename all instances of ExampleEngine to AmbientWaves Add the required header files needed, for ambient waves only math.h is needed #include "math.h" Add the ambient waves paremeters to the class definition in AmbientWaves.h : float velocity = 0.1 ; float amplitude = 0.25 ; float period = 0.2 ; float angle = M_PI / 2 ; Register them in populateTable method of AmbientWaves.cpp so they can be sent over OSC and shown in the dashboard tb . add ( "velocity" , & velocity , {. min = 0 , . max = 2 , . step = 0.01 }); tb . add ( "angle" , & angle , {. min = 0 , . max = 2 * M_PI , . step = 0.01 }); tb . add ( "period" , & period , {. min = 0 , . max = 1 , . step = 0.01 }); tb . add ( "amplitude" , & amplitude , {. min = 0 , . max = 1 , . step = 0.01 }); The influence part of the influence engine is calculate in the influenceOn method Register Influence Engine in base LASG code ¶ Compile firmware ¶ Compiling A WASM Influence Engine ¶ Create & compile WASM Influence Engine wrapper To recompile an existing WASM Influence engine. Run zig build in the firmware directory. This will build all IE's in the zig.build config file and save the compiled WASMs to the server/public directory. To add a new IE to the zig build step, add a buildWasm() call to to the pub fn build(b: *std.Build) function. For example, the ambient waves build function looks like: buildWasm(b, "AmbientWaves", &.{ "AmbientWaves.cpp", "AmbientWavesWasm.cpp", }, optimize); Register the Influence Engine’s wasm binary in the dashboard GUI ¶ Specify basic tools and components Implement specific IE visualization [ tbd ]

docs.text: Advanced Testbed Setup ¶ For complex testbeds, testbed data can be authored in an external 3D modeling software such as Blender, and uploaded to the server via the LASD file format. Testbed Data: Testbed data describes the spatial locations, and metadata that describe the actuators, sensors & node controllers that make up a testbed. This data is provided using the "Living Architecture Systems Description" (LASD) format. Testbed Image: The testbed image is the background image displayed in the Influence Engine dashboard. 1) Authoring Testbed Data: ¶ Testbed Data in the LASD format can be authored in the 3D modeling tools Blender or Rhino and exported using the LASD plugins (install information for LASD plugins can be found here ). To export Testbed Data directly from Blender to an Aether Database configure the following settings in the LASD Database panel: Database URL: The URL of your Aether Server instance Database Name: The name of your Aether Database Database Path: The name of the Testbed you want to export this LASD data too Auth Port: The authorization port for your Aether Database (Default is typically 9099) Database Port: The port for the Aether Database (Default is typically 9000) API Key: The API Key for your Aether Database Username: The username for your account in your Aether Database Password: The password for your account in your Aether Database Once those setting have been configured, use the Export to Database button to export this testbed to the Database. Troubleshooting Export Errors If there are errors with the export, try running the Sanitize Names for Database Export command, this will attempt to replace any invalid characters that cause issues when exporting ( Blender .### suffix on object names is typically the culprit here ) 2) Adding a Testbed Plan Image: ¶ To add a custom background image that will display in the Aether Dashboard: Create a plan view image plan view can be created in the tool of your testbed in the tool of your choice. The image must be saved as a .png. Note When creating a background image, ensure that the image is drawn using the same pixel:meter scale as defined in the testbed Metadata. Add the image to the Aether Server: plan images should be located in the server/public/plan_images folder and be named with the following format [YOUR TESTBED NAME]_plan.png

docs.text: pip ## Coordinate Spaces When writing draw functions in the Aether Dashboard. It's helpful to understand the 3 co-ordinate spaces used in dashboardP5.js World Space: the "Real World" coordinates of objects 3D Left Handed +Z Up +Y Forward (+Y up in plan view) +X Right coordinate system. Measured in mm. The origin of the World Coordinate space is typically defined by the origin point of the tool that authored the Testbed LASD data (typically the Blender or Rhino world origin). Grid Space: 3D Left Handed +Z Up, +Y Backwards (+Y Down in plan view) +X Right coordinate system. (we don't really use the z much here, but grid space is still 3D) Grid space is measured in pixels, The Testbed background image should be centered exactly in grid space Origin defined by the plan_offset key in the testbed metadata, Pixel Scale (relative to world space) defined by the plan_ratio key in the testbed metadata ( ratio of pixels to mm ) The maximum extents of the grid space is determined by the size of the testbed background image (in px) and our minimum zoom value. Canvas Space: this is our "viewport" into grid space: Canvas Space extents are determined by the actual canvas size on the webpage. Canvas Space origin is offset from grid space by the p5 grid properties xoff and yoff . (Panning) Scaled relative to Grid Space by the zoom value. Conversion Functions ¶ The following conversion functions, located in dashboardP5.js can be used to convert between the Coordinate spaces: worldToGridCoords([x,y,z]) -> {x:x,y:y,z:z} gridToWorldCoords({x:x,y:y,z:z}) -> {x:x,y:y,z:z} canvasToGridCoords({x:x,y:y},z,p5 instance) -> {x:x,y:y,z:z} Also the worldMouse() function on the P5 instance can be called to return the current mouse position in World Space.

docs.text: Hooks & Signals ¶ Signals are used to automatically update UI components when the state of the application changes. Signals in Aether's UI make use of Preact's Hooks and Signals , as well as Aether's Observable object to simplify creating UI components that are sync'd with Aether's Database. Each type of Signal references a Observable object and a key which defines the value on the State Proxy object that is being listened to, or changed. When to Use Signals Signals should be used in contexts where the current state of the application needs to be kept in sync with the database, but there is no re-occurring update loop. For contexts with an update loop, like a p5.js canvas, us a get() (or one of the get helpers) instead. When to Use use Each signal described below has a memoized varient use<SingalName> . These memoized hooks can only be used within Preact function components. When creating a signal outside of a Preact component, use the standard version of the signal not the use<SingalName> , version. objectSignal(): ¶ objectSignal takes a Preact Signal, a Observable object and a Key. When the value at the specified Key is changed (say by a UI component using an objectSignal) the signal updates the State Proxy object, which then updates the database. If the Key that the objectSignal is listening to is updated in the database the signal value will be updated as well. The useObjetSignal function takes only the Observable object and Key, and creates a memoized objectSignal. errorSignal(): ¶ errorSignal takes a Preact Signal, a Observable object, and a Key. Like objectSignal, when the value at the specified Key is changed (say by a UI component using an the errorSignal) the signal updates the State Proxy object, which then updates the database. If the Key that the errorSignal is listening to is updated in the database the signal value will be updated as well. an errorSignal also keeps track of whether or not its Observable object was successful in updating the database. If updating the database was unsuccessful, then the error signal reverts the Observable's local value back to the last successfully set value. If the dependency is undefined the dependentSignal will be in a loading state and also be undefined until the dependency resolves to a value. After loading, if the value of the dependency changes the dependentSignal recomputes the getObj expression to return a Observable object based on the dependencies new value. The recomputed value of the dependentSignal will then be the Key's corresponding value in the returned Observable object. The useDependentSignal function creates a memoized dependentSignal. If live is false currentSetting("CloudGen") returns the object at <TESTBED>.transient.sessions.<SESSION_ID>.CloudGen . Preact ¶ See the preact docs for more info (note the preact docs use jsx in most places its quite similar to htm but uses {} instead of ${}) HTM and Preact are Javascript libraries that help with creating UI components. To be able to have reusable components (switches, sliders, etc.) we want some way to create a function that can contain all the logic and markup to render this component. The way we do this is with preact and htm. We use htm to create the markup, it useless a tagged template literal a template literal is just a javascript string that can include interpolations (javascript expressions within them) for example for an untagged template: const string = `
hello ${ 1 }
` string == "
hello 1
" the tagged template literal from htm allows us to write regular html as well as including javascript within it using the interpolations ( ${} ). The element’s children and attributes that you write get passed to preact for rendering. Preact then uses that structure to create a virtual dom (vdom), a tree of the nodes and their attributes and children similar to the dom in the browser. This vdom can then be rendered within a parent element with the render function. To create a component you create a normal javascript function that takes an object with the attributes that can be set on it (sometimes called properties, or props). This component can be included in any html template like so: html ` < ${ Component } attribute1="test">

child element

Where Component is defined as: function Component ({ attribute1 , children }) { return html `
${ children }
` } Components functions can have other logic and such within them, and when any of their attributes/props change they cause a re-render. This re-render only changes the vdom, not the actual webpage. Then preact will figure out what changed and then make those changes to the page https://preactjs.com/guide/v10/getting-started and the tutorial for more info Preact Signals ¶ https://preactjs.com/guide/v10/signals signal.value and effect ¶ In concept a signal is just an object with a value key that signals some ui or functions when that value changes. To create a signal you use const num = signal(1) and then access the value with num.value Then one way to have a function that responds to this signal is with the effect function. The effect function runs the callback given to it and tracks which signals were accessed; when those signals values have changed, it reruns the function, the next function is computed which takes a callback to compute a new value from one or more signals and returns a readonly signal whose value will be recomputed whenever the signals it depends on changes. Reactive UI ¶ Just like how props changing can cause preact to rerender, if signals are used in an html template it will cause preact to rerender. Signals also create another way to do a “fine grained” update to the ui if you pass the signal object instead of the object.value preact won’t cause a rerender(calling the component function again to regenerate the virtual dom to be diffed). Some of our components take signals as attributes this allows to easily integrate with our wrapped signals for having sliders or toggles be automatically integrated with the database Hooks and wrapped signals ¶ To use signals with preact, we have to use hooks. This is because we want to use the same signal on rerenders, when creating a signal from a component we use the useSignal function which returns the same signal on each render(under the hood it uses the useMemo hook). One common way to use signals is to wrap them to add more functionality to them; this allows for integration with the database and state proxy.

docs.text: Getting Started with Aether ¶ This guide walks through the basic operation of Aether's Dashboard, Node Configuration, and Logic Reactor, to setup a device with simple responsive behaviour. Setup from Scratch If you are setting up Aether from scratch, please see the Server Setup and Node Controller Setup pages. If you are participating in a workshop or working with an existing Testbed then a Server and set of Node Controllers will already be in place. Accessing Aether Web UI ¶ To access Aethers web interfaces, connect a computer or laptop to the "Aether-Local" Wifi network, open Google Chrome web browser and enter the following in the address bar 172.23.4.1:3022 This will bring you to the Aether Log-In page: From this page you can log in, if you have previously registered an account with this server, or Register a new account. Aether's Dashboard ¶ After logging in or registering you will have access to Aethers web interface. The first page you will see is Aether's Dashboard. Aether's Dashboard allows you to manage the arrangement of Node Controllers , Devices that Aether can interact with, as well as the parameters of Influence Engines , weather-like environmental algorithms that impact each devices behaviour. Connecting and Positioning New Node Controllers. ¶ Once a new device is powered on and connects to the Aether Server, it will be added to the origin point of the dashboard. Once the Node Controller appears in the dashboard, it can be dragged and dropped into the desired position. if you can't drag and drop to move Node Controllers, make sure that the "Lock Positions" toggle in unchecked in the bottom left settings bar Subscribing to an Influence Engine ¶ To test that your new device is communicating with Aether, we will try subscribing it to the Ambient Waves Influence Engine . Subscribing a device to an influence engine allows it to be sensitive to, and respond to, changes in that Influence Engine. Subscribing to Ambient Waves in the Dashboard Effects of Subscribing to Ambient Waves To read more about the variety of Influence Engines available with Aether, see the Influence Engines Section of the documentation. Configuring a Node Controller ¶ A Node Controllers configuration and placement of Actuators in Aether should accurately reflect the physical layout of actuators in the real world. To arrange and configure a Node Controller, we can use the Node Configuration Editor In the Node Configuration Editor you can drag and drop components from the left side menu to create an arrangement of actuators, and connect those actuators to a Node Controller. To configure a Node controller: 1) Make note of the Node Controllers ID number in the Dashboard. 2) Go to the Node Configuration page, 3) Select the Node ID in the Select NC Dropdown 4) Drag and Drop a Node Controller block into the workspace. 5) Drag and Drop Devices into the workspace Device parameters, such as the devices type, can be configured in the Device Parameters side menu 6) Connect each device to the desired port on the Node Controller Block 7) Use the export button to export the configuration for this Node Controller to the Database Behaviour Logic ¶ So far we have setup a Node Controller to react passively to the external Influence Engine algorithms. To create more complete behaviors, we can use the Logic Reactor editor to create internal behaviours for a Node Controller. The Logic Reactor is also where we can configure which sensors are connected to a Node Controller, and how those sensor inputs are used. The Logic editior is a visual scripting environment where logic blocks can be chained together to create complex behaviour. A block may have inputs (located on their top or left sides), outputs (located on their right or bottom sides), as well as some parameters (located in the block parameter side menu). In this getting started guide we will configure the logic editor take sensor input from the Sensor Expansion hub, and use that sensor input to trigger a cascading set of lights. For a more comprehensive list of Logic Blocks and their functionality, see the Logic Reactor page of the documentation. To configure a sensor to trigger outputs on a Node Controller: Testing Sensor Input ¶ Ensure the node controller is powered on, with an IR Sensor plugged into the first port of the Sensor Expansion Hub Make note of the Node Controllers ID number in the Dashboard. Go to the Logic Reactor page, Select the Node ID in the Select NC Dropdown Save a preset with a name of your choice Drag and Drop a Node Controller block into the workspace. Drag and Drop a Sensor Hub block into the workspace Drag a Number Output block into the workspace Connect the first port of the sensor hub to the Number output block Check that the output value changes when you move your hand in front of the sensor Note If you aren't seeing output from the Sensor Hub, make sure you have the correct Node Controller selected, and try hitting the upload button. If the block still isn't responding, try hitting the Reset TCP button in the Hardware -> Troubleshooting Tools menu on the dashboard. Setup a Basic Trigger ¶ Drag a Trigger Threshold block into the workspace. Drag a Sequence Playback block into the workspace. Connect the first output of the Sensor Hub to the input of the Trigger Threshold Block, Connect the output of the Trigger Threshold block to the input of the Sequence Playback block. Connect the Output of the Sequence Playback block to the first input of the NC block. Add a Level Visualizer and connect it to the first output of the NC block Moving your hand in front of the sensor should now cause the first Actuator of the Node Controller to playback a sequence. Editing Sequences ¶ You can edit the sequences used in the Sequence Playback block by going to the Block Parameters menu and selecting the Edit Sequence button Cascading Sequences ¶ You can create a cascade of sequences by using the Propagation block to offset the playback of multiple sequences. Using Virtual Inputs ¶ If your prototyping behaviour without a Node Controller connected, you can use the Virtual Input Buttons to simulate Sensor inputs Try combining logic blocks in unique ways to see what kinds of behaviour you can create.

docs.text: Logic Reactor ¶ The Logic Reactor defines the internal logic of a Node Controller, and provides a graph based interface to configure logical operations and behaviours. Graph Settings ¶ The Graph Settings panel shows the currently selected graph, and Node Controller. Block Parameters ¶ The Block Parameters panel shows the parameters that can be adjusted on the selected block. Individual block parameters are described in detail in the Blocks Section below, but some features are common to all blocks: Surfaced: The Surfaced toggle determines whether or not this blocks parameters are made visible in the dashboard. A Node Controller's surfaced parameters appear in the Hardware panel when it is selected in the dashboard. Blocks ¶ Software Inputs ¶ Software Input blocks create continuous inputs to the logic graph. These inputs can be manipulate via the Logic Editor user interface, or Surfaced to be made visible in the Hardware Panel of the Dashboard. Button: ¶ The button block provides a momentary input of 1.0 when pressed in the Logic Editor. When not pressed the button provides an input of 0.0. Slider: ¶ The slider provides a continuous input between 0.0 and 1.0 depending on how it is set. Grab the handle to adjust the value in the Logic Editor. Switch: ¶ The switch provides a continuous input of 0.0 or 1.0 depending on its state. Click the switch in the Logic Editor to toggle its state. Integer: ¶ The integer input provides a continuous integer value. Use the plus or minus buttons in the Logic Editor to adjust its value. External Inputs ¶ Hardware Inputs are driven from the Analog & Digital sensor readings on a Node Controller. When a Node Controller is selected in the Touch: ¶ The Touch block provides input from the Capacitive Touch sensor of the Node controller. The touch block also provides parameter to remap the raw touch values from the Node controller to a 0.0 to 1.0 range: Name Description rest The Baseline touch value, use the "Set Rest" button to set this value when nothing is touching the capacitive touch sensor hard The Maximum touch value, use the "Set Hard" button to set this value while firmly gripping the capacitive touch sensor interpolation Not yet used Analog Sensor: ¶ The Analog Sensor block provides input from the Analog Sensor attached to the Node Controller. This block also provides parameters to remap the sensor range: Name Description floor The Baseline value, used for remapping ceiling The Maximum touch value, used for remapping Influence: ¶ The Influence Input provides the current influence of the selected Influence Engine on this Node Controller ( Modulated by the Node Controllers React Ability's Subscription level ) Message Input: ¶ The message input allows the Node controller to listen for input over OSC. The key parameter allows you to define the OSC address this block should listen to. Messages with the address format /logic/[key] will be received by this block. Sensor Hub: ¶ Used with the Node Controller Sensor Hub Expansion board, provides 6 additional ADC inputs, via I2C Operators ¶ Trigger Threshold: ¶ Trigger threshold sets a threshold value that must be reached before a value is emitted. Note the trigger value is equal to the input value, as long as the input value is above the trigger Threshold. The Tigger Threshold block has the following parameters: Name Description trigThreshold Threshold value above which this block outputs a trigger value trigReset Value below which the latch resets flagTrigLatch If enabled, the input value must drop below the trigRest value before this block will output another trigger value. trigCooldownMs Defines a cooldown time between the output of trigger values. Using Trigger Threshold to create a momentary trigger from a continuous input value Sequence: ¶ The Sequence operator plays back a user defined sequence when it receives an Input. Use the Edit Sequence in the block parameters to draw a new sequence. Sequence demo Propagation: ¶ A delay. The propagation operator starts a timeline when it receives an input, at the specified point on the timeline it outputs an attenuated trigger value. Simple Propagation Demo Using Propagation to create a chain of sequences Math: ¶ The math operator allows you to select a math operation to be done on it's two input values. The available operations are: Symbol Desciption + Addition - Subtraction X Multiplication ÷ Division Note: Division by 0 will return Infinity % Modulo > Greater Than Note: Returns 1.0 if True, 0.0 if False < Less Than Note: Returns 1.0 if True, 0.0 if False == Is Equal To Note: Returns 1.0 if True, 0.0 if False != Is Not Equal To Note: Returns 1.0 if True, 0.0 if False MAX Maximum. Returns the greater of the two values MIN Minimum. Returns the lesser of the two values Outputs ¶ Node Controller: ¶ The Node Controller block lets the graph control the actuators attached to a Node Controller, Each Input corresponds to one of the Actuator port on the Node Controller. The Outputs can be used to visualize the output of each port. Level Visualizer: ¶ Provides visual feedback representing the input value. Value Display: ¶ Displays the input value as text Subscription: ¶ Can be used to modify the Subscription levels of this Node Controller. The input will set the subscription level for the Influence Engine and Ability specified. Organization ¶ Comments: ¶ Can be used to place comments throughout a logic graph.

docs.text: Node Configuration ¶ The Node Configuration Editor allows you to setup which actuators are connected to a Node Controller, and how they are arranged spatially. In the Node Configuration Editor you can drag and drop components from the left side menu to create an arrangement of actuators, and connect those actuators to a Node Controller to assign them to the connected actuator port. Node Menu ¶ General Settings such as the current preset, and currently selected Node Controller can be found in the Node Menu. This menu also lists the IP Address and MAC address of the currently selected Node Controller. The Export Button will export the current configuration to the Node Controller. Device Parameters Menu ¶ The Device Parameters Menu allows you to change the properties of the currently Selected Device. Here you can select the Devices Type (Light, Vibration or Motor) as well as set the devices Z_HEIGHT, which is the height of the device above floor level in millimeters. Blocks ¶ 3 types of blocks can be dragged and dropped into the configuration workspace: Devices: ¶ Devices can be positioned in space and connected to the Node Controller Block to define which Actuator Pin they are connected too. Devices can be one of 3 types Light, Vibration or Motor. The device type can be set in the Device Parameters Menu. Node Controller: ¶ The Node Controller block has 6 Actuator pins which devices can be connected to. The Node Controller also defines the origin of the layout space, all device positions are relative to the Node Controller block. Warning Only one Node Controller block should be added to the workspace, adding more than 1 Node Controller block to the workspace can cause export errors. Pegboard Guides: ¶ The Pegboard guides provide a reference image of the LASG Kit Pegboards to use as a scale reference when laying out devices. Both the Hex Pegboard and Tri Pegboard are provided, and the type can be toggled by selecting a Pegboard guide and using the dropdown in the Device Parameters Menu.

docs.text: Connecting External Tools ¶ This guide explains how to inject Influence Engine events into Aether from any tool that can send OSC UDP — Python scripts, microcontrollers (CircuitPython, MicroPython), Max MSP patches, and similar. Typical use cases: - A microcontroller reading a radar sensor and emitting createPresence events at detected positions - A Max MSP patch that responds to audio energy by triggering createPulse events - A Python script driving pheromone trails from algorithmic or generative data Network Setup ¶ Each Node Controller (NC) listens directly for OSC on UDP port 1212 . Events must be sent to the broadcast address of your subnet — either 255.255.255.255 (global broadcast) or the subnet broadcast address (e.g. 192.168.1.255 ). This is what ensures all NCs on the network receive the event simultaneously. Do not send to the server's IP address for normal use — the server does not forward events to the NCs. Sending to the server IP will reach the server only, not the NCs. Your sending machine must be on the same subnet as the NCs. Exception — recording sessions: If you need the server to capture events for replay during a performance recording, send to the server's IP address using the path /server/<EngineName>/sendEvent . The server logs the event and rebroadcasts it to all NCs. All other message details are identical. This is only needed when recording. OSC Message Format ¶ Every event follows this structure: OSC address: /<EngineName>/sendEvent Arguments: 1. eventName — string — the name of the event Repeated key–value pairs: paramName — string paramValue — int or float (type matters — see each engine's table below) All positions for Influence Engine events are in World Space millimetres . You can find the world-space coordinates of a Node by right-clicking on it in the Dashboard plan. For details on how Aether's World Space coordinates are oriented see the Coordinate Spaces RadiantPulse — createPulse ¶ A radiant pulse is an expanding ring (or sphere) that propagates outward from a point and fades over its lifespan. Pulses accumulate: multiple simultaneous pulses sum at each location, clamped to 0–1. OSC address: /RadiantPulse/sendEvent Event name: createPulse Parameter Type Unit Default Range Description x int mm (required) — Origin X y int mm (required) — Origin Y z int mm (required) — Origin Z core int mm 100 — Radius of the solid inner core size int mm 600 100–1500 Outer radius at emission speed float m/s 1.5 0–3 Expansion speed lifespan int ms 4500 50–5000 Time until the pulse is removed strength float 0–1 0.8 0–1 Peak influence fadeRatio float 0–1 0.7 0–1 Fraction of lifespan spent fading spherical int 0/1 1 — 1 = 3D sphere, 0 = planar ring x , y , z are required. Omitted optional parameters fall back to the NC's current RadiantPulse settings. Presence — createPresence ¶ A presence event places a Gaussian influence field at a point. Fields from multiple events sum together and fade individually. The influence vector points radially outward from each event's position — actuators are pushed away from detected presences. OSC address: /Presence/sendEvent Event name: createPresence Parameter Type Unit Default Range Description x int mm (required) — Centre X y int mm (required) — Centre Y z int mm (required) — Centre Z sigma float mm 400 50–3000 Gaussian spread (standard deviation) strength float 0–1 0.8 0–1 Peak influence at centre lifespan int ms 3000 100–10000 Time until the field is removed fadeRatio float 0–1 0.5 0–1 Fraction of lifespan spent fading spherical int 0/1 0 — 1 = 3D Gaussian falloff, 0 = planar For a person-tracking use case, send one event per detected person per sensor frame (e.g. at 10 Hz for the LD2450 radar). With lifespan = 3000ms and fadeRatio = 0.5, a presence field lingers 1.5 seconds after the person leaves the frame. Pheromone — createPheromone ¶ A pheromone event places a Gaussian field that can attract actuators toward the source or repel them away. Pheromone trails accumulate naturally when events are sent at a position repeatedly — they are long-lived by design. The influence vector points toward the event position for positive (attracting) pheromones, and away for negative (repelling) ones. OSC address: /Pheromone/sendEvent Event name: createPheromone Parameter Type Unit Default Range Description x int mm (required) — Centre X y int mm (required) — Centre Y z int mm (required) — Centre Z sigma float mm 600 50–3000 Gaussian spread strength float 0–0.5 0.05 0–0.5 Influence magnitude positive int 0/1 1 — 1 = attracting (toward source), 0 = repelling lifespan int ms 10000 100–30000 Time until the field is removed fadeRatio float 0–1 0.3 0–1 Fraction of lifespan spent fading spherical int 0/1 0 — 1 = 3D falloff, 0 = planar strength is always a positive magnitude (0–0.5); the direction of effect is set by positive . Low strength values (0.05–0.1) work well for trails because fields accumulate with each event sent. Python Examples ¶ Install python-osc : pip install python-osc One-shot events ¶ from pythonosc.udp_client import SimpleUDPClient # Broadcast to all NCs on the network client = SimpleUDPClient ( "255.255.255.255" , 1212 , allow_broadcast = True ) # RadiantPulse client . send_message ( "/RadiantPulse/sendEvent" , [ "createPulse" , "x" , 1500 , "y" , 2000 , "z" , 0 , "size" , 800 , "speed" , 1.5 , "lifespan" , 4500 , "strength" , 0.8 , "fadeRatio" , 0.7 , "spherical" , 1 , ]) # Presence client . send_message ( "/Presence/sendEvent" , [ "createPresence" , "x" , 3200 , "y" , 1100 , "z" , 900 , "sigma" , 400.0 , "strength" , 0.8 , "lifespan" , 3000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.5 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) # Pheromone (attracting trail) client . send_message ( "/Pheromone/sendEvent" , [ "createPheromone" , "x" , 2000 , "y" , 1500 , "z" , 0 , "sigma" , 600.0 , "strength" , 0.1 , "positive" , 1 , "lifespan" , 10000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.3 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) Type notes: python-osc infers OSC types from Python types: int → OSC integer, float → OSC float, str → OSC string. Write 400.0 not 400 for float parameters, and use plain int values for x , y , z , lifespan , spherical , and positive . Continuous presence tracking loop ¶ This pattern fits a sensor that reports detected positions at a fixed rate (e.g. an LD2450 radar at 10 Hz): import time from pythonosc.udp_client import SimpleUDPClient client = SimpleUDPClient ( "255.255.255.255" , 1212 , allow_broadcast = True ) SENSOR_HEIGHT_MM = 900 # Z height of detected persons while True : targets = read_sensor () # returns list of (x_mm, y_mm) in LASD world space for x , y in targets : client . send_message ( "/Presence/sendEvent" , [ "createPresence" , "x" , int ( x ), "y" , int ( y ), "z" , SENSOR_HEIGHT_MM , "sigma" , 400.0 , "strength" , 0.8 , "lifespan" , 3000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.5 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) time . sleep ( 0.1 ) # 10 Hz Pheromone trail from a moving object ¶ Dropping pheromone events at each position in a path builds a trail. With low strength and long lifespan , the trail accumulates and fades slowly: for x , y in path_positions : client . send_message ( "/Pheromone/sendEvent" , [ "createPheromone" , "x" , int ( x ), "y" , int ( y ), "z" , 0 , "sigma" , 600.0 , "strength" , 0.05 , # low — trail accumulates "positive" , 1 , "lifespan" , 10000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.3 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) time . sleep ( 0.05 ) # 20 Hz Max MSP Examples ¶ Max MSP sends OSC using [oscformat] → [udpsend] . In Max messages, an atom without a decimal is an integer; with a decimal it is a float. Parameters like speed , sigma , strength , and fadeRatio must have a decimal point (e.g. 1.5 , 400. , 0.8 ). Parameters like x , y , z , lifespan , spherical , and positive must be plain integers. Basic patch structure ¶ [message] | [oscformat] | [udpsend 255.255.255.255 1212] [udpsend] must be opened with the broadcast address before use — either send it a connect 255.255.255.255 1212 message, or include it as arguments: [udpsend 255.255.255.255 1212] . RadiantPulse ¶ Static message box: /RadiantPulse/sendEvent createPulse x 1500 y 2000 z 0 size 800 speed 1.5 lifespan 4500 strength 0.8 fadeRatio 0.7 spherical 1 [screenshot — static RadiantPulse patch] Presence ¶ Static message box: /Presence/sendEvent createPresence x 3200 y 1100 z 900 sigma 400. strength 0.8 lifespan 3000 fadeRatio 0.5 spherical 0 [screenshot — static Presence patch] For a dynamic patch where position comes from number boxes or a tracking source, use [sprintf] to substitute x, y, z at send time: [number x] [number y] [number z] Connect these to the inlets of: [sprintf /Presence/sendEvent createPresence x %i y %i z %i sigma 400. strength 0.8 lifespan 3000 fadeRatio 0.5 spherical 0] The %i specifiers keep the substituted values as integers. The fixed float parameters ( 400. , 0.8 , etc.) remain as float atoms in the output list. [screenshot — dynamic Presence patch with number boxes and sprintf] Pheromone ¶ Static message box (attracting): /Pheromone/sendEvent createPheromone x 2000 y 1500 z 0 sigma 600. strength 0.1 positive 1 lifespan 10000 fadeRatio 0.3 spherical 0 To toggle between attracting and repelling, route a [toggle] into a [select 0 1] → two message boxes: /Pheromone/sendEvent createPheromone x 2000 y 1500 z 0 sigma 600. strength 0.1 positive 1 lifespan 10000 fadeRatio 0.3 spherical 0 /Pheromone/sendEvent createPheromone x 2000 y 1500 z 0 sigma 600. strength 0.1 positive 0 lifespan 10000 fadeRatio 0.3 spherical 0 [screenshot — Pheromone patch with attract/repel toggle]

docs.text: from pythonosc.udp_client import SimpleUDPClient # Broadcast to all NCs on the network client = SimpleUDPClient ( "255.255.255.255" , 1212 , allow_broadcast = True ) # RadiantPulse client . send_message ( "/RadiantPulse/sendEvent" , [ "createPulse" , "x" , 1500 , "y" , 2000 , "z" , 0 , "size" , 800 , "speed" , 1.5 , "lifespan" , 4500 , "strength" , 0.8 , "fadeRatio" , 0.7 , "spherical" , 1 , ]) # Presence client . send_message ( "/Presence/sendEvent" , [ "createPresence" , "x" , 3200 , "y" , 1100 , "z" , 900 , "sigma" , 400.0 , "strength" , 0.8 , "lifespan" , 3000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.5 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) # Pheromone (attracting trail) client . send_message ( "/Pheromone/sendEvent" , [ "createPheromone" , "x" , 2000 , "y" , 1500 , "z" , 0 , "sigma" , 600.0 , "strength" , 0.1 , "positive" , 1 , "lifespan" , 10000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.3 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) Type notes: python-osc infers OSC types from Python types: int → OSC integer, float → OSC float, str → OSC string. Write 400.0 not 400 for float parameters, and use plain int values for x , y , z , lifespan , spherical , and positive .

docs.text: This pattern fits a sensor that reports detected positions at a fixed rate (e.g. an LD2450 radar at 10 Hz): import time from pythonosc.udp_client import SimpleUDPClient client = SimpleUDPClient ( "255.255.255.255" , 1212 , allow_broadcast = True ) SENSOR_HEIGHT_MM = 900 # Z height of detected persons while True : targets = read_sensor () # returns list of (x_mm, y_mm) in LASD world space for x , y in targets : client . send_message ( "/Presence/sendEvent" , [ "createPresence" , "x" , int ( x ), "y" , int ( y ), "z" , SENSOR_HEIGHT_MM , "sigma" , 400.0 , "strength" , 0.8 , "lifespan" , 3000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.5 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) time . sleep ( 0.1 ) # 10 Hz

docs.text: Dropping pheromone events at each position in a path builds a trail. With low strength and long lifespan , the trail accumulates and fades slowly: for x , y in path_positions : client . send_message ( "/Pheromone/sendEvent" , [ "createPheromone" , "x" , int ( x ), "y" , int ( y ), "z" , 0 , "sigma" , 600.0 , "strength" , 0.05 , # low — trail accumulates "positive" , 1 , "lifespan" , 10000 , "fadeRatio" , 0.3 , "spherical" , 0 , ]) time . sleep ( 0.05 ) # 20 Hz

docs.text: Max MSP sends OSC using [oscformat] → [udpsend] . In Max messages, an atom without a decimal is an integer; with a decimal it is a float. Parameters like speed , sigma , strength , and fadeRatio must have a decimal point (e.g. 1.5 , 400. , 0.8 ). Parameters like x , y , z , lifespan , spherical , and positive must be plain integers.

docs.text: [message] | [oscformat] | [udpsend 255.255.255.255 1212] [udpsend] must be opened with the broadcast address before use — either send it a connect 255.255.255.255 1212 message, or include it as arguments: [udpsend 255.255.255.255 1212] .

docs.text: Static message box: /Presence/sendEvent createPresence x 3200 y 1100 z 900 sigma 400. strength 0.8 lifespan 3000 fadeRatio 0.5 spherical 0 [screenshot — static Presence patch] For a dynamic patch where position comes from number boxes or a tracking source, use [sprintf] to substitute x, y, z at send time: [number x] [number y] [number z] Connect these to the inlets of: [sprintf /Presence/sendEvent createPresence x %i y %i z %i sigma 400. strength 0.8 lifespan 3000 fadeRatio 0.5 spherical 0] The %i specifiers keep the substituted values as integers. The fixed float parameters ( 400. , 0.8 , etc.) remain as float atoms in the output list. [screenshot — dynamic Presence patch with number boxes and sprintf]

docs.text: Custom Server ¶ Cloning Aethers Testbed-v4 Repository from Github ¶ Ask for access to https://github.com/pbarch/testbed-v4 and clone it with git clone https://github.com/pbarch/testbed-v4 Setting Up Node.js & NPM ¶ Nodejs is used for running the server and firebase database. To easily manage Nodejs version we reccomend installing Node Version Manager (NVM) . With NVM installed you can use nvm install --lts to install the latest long term support version of Nodejs and NPM. Alternatively you can directly install a version of nodejs and npm from https://nodejs.org/en/download/prebuilt-installer if desired. Once Nodejs and npm are installed, open a terminal in the testbed-v4\server folder and install the dependencies required to run the Aether Server with: npm install Note The firebase emulator also requires the Java SDK (version 21 or above) to be installed. You can find an installer for your platform on Oracles Java Downloads Page Running the Server. ¶ In the testbed-v4\server folder, run node server.mjs to start the server. Once the server is running you can access Aether locally at http://localhost:3022/ or on your network at http://[YOUR IP ADDRESS]:3022 Configuration ¶ You can modifiy the default IP addreses for external systems (Light, Sound, Projection etc.) as well as setting related to the firebase database in the aether_default.env file.

docs.text: Node Controller Setup ¶ To start using Aether, you will need a running Aether Server as well as some Aether Node Controllers Note If you are interacting with Aether as part of a workshop or established Testbed, an Aether Server and Node Controllers may already be configured for you, in these cases you can skip ahead to the Getting Started section of the documentation. Creating a Node Controller ¶ The distributed devices interact with Aether are called Node Controllers. A Node Controller can be created using the LASG's custom Node Controller boards, or by compiling firmware to an off the shelf ESP32 Microcontroller, such as an Adafruit Huzzah or Seeed Studio XIAO board. Configuration ¶ Before compiling a Node Controller's firmware, we need to setup its configuration file, so that the new Node Controller will have the necessary information to connect to a Wifi Network, and the Aether Server. These configuration settings are defined in the aether_config.h file, found in the firmware folder of the testbed-v4 repository. If you have just cloned the repository from github, you may not have an aether_config.h file, you can create one by copying the aether_config_template.h file. For a standalone Aether Server the aether_config.h file should contain the following: #define USE_TELNET #define WIFI_SSID_ROUTER "Aether-Local" #define WIFI_PWD_ROUTER [PASSWORD] #define WIFI_PREFERRED WIFI_SSID_ROUTER #define IP_1(X) 172 // The First Octet of the IP Address #define IP_2(X) 23 // The Second Octet of the IP Address #define IP_3(X) 4 // The Third Octet of the IP Address #define SERVER_IP(X) "172.23.4.1" #define MQTT_ADDR_LOCAL(X) "172.23.4.1" Where [PASSWORD] is the password setup / provided for the Raspberry Pi's Wifi Access Point. First Time Firmware Compilation ¶ Note Compiling Firmware for a Node Controller Requires Zig and PlatformIO to be installed. For Instructions on installing Zig and PlatformIO for a standalone server see Setting up the Build System To compile firmware directly to a supported device. Connect the device to the computer / Raspberry Pi running Aether using a micro usb cable. Open a terminal in the firmware folder of Aethers testbed-v4 repository. run pio run -e [DEVICE ID] --target upload where [DEVICE ID] is replaced by the following identifier depending on the connected device Microcontroller [DEVICE ID] Adafruit Huzzah Feather S1 featheresp32 LASG Node Controller Version 1.7 adafruit_feather_esp32s3 Seeed Studio Xiao Esp32s3 seeed_xiao_esp32s3 This will compile the firmware and upload it to the device. After restarting, a node controller should connect to the Aether-Local Wifi network, and the Aether Server, and become visible on the Dashboard Troubleshooting Devices: ¶ Right clicking on a device in the dashboard will show you its IP address. With Its IP address you can connect to the device from a command prompt or terminal via telnet: telnet [DEVICE IP] This will give you a print out of the devices debug outputs. There are 3 levels of debug information that can be cycled through by entering "d" into the telnet terminal.

docs.text: Aether Server Setup - Options ¶ To start using Aether, you will need a running Aether Server as well as some Aether Node Controllers . Note If you are interacting with Aether as part of a workshop or established Testbed, an Aether Server and Node Controllers may already be configured for you, in these cases you can skip ahead to the Getting Started section of the documentation. If you are setting up an Aether Server yourself, you can proceed with 1 of 2 options: 1) Standalone Server A standalone server will run an Aether on a Raspberry Pi, and host a local Wifi network that devices can connect to. 2) Custom Server A custom server can run on a device of your choice and be configured to work on an existing network configuration.

docs.text: Standalone Server - Raspberry Pi ¶ Initial Setup ¶ A standalone Server can be quickly created using a pre-made Raspberry Pi image. (Contact PBSI for access to a pre built image) This Image can be flashed to a 32GB SD card using the Raspberry Pi imager. The image has been tested with a Raspberry Pi 5 (4GB RAM) and a Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB of RAM). The Pi is configured with a desktop environment but should be able to be used primarily remotely without a display, mouse or keyboard. After starting up the PI a new WiFi network will appear called "Aether-Local". Connecting to this network will give you access to Aether. If the Pi is also connected to the internet via Ethernet then the wireless Aether-Local network will also provide internet access. Once a device is connected to the Aether-Local network it can access the Aether interface by opening a web browser (preferably Chrome) and going to: http://aether:3022/ this should open the Aether Login page: An administrator user will be configured for you and credentials provided with the pre-built image. Once logged in you can navigate to the Dashboard Panel to see connected Node Controllers. Adding Node Controllers. ¶ Aether's Node Controllers are the distributed devices co-ordinated by the Aether interface. Custom Node Controller PCB's developed by PBSI can be used, or an Adafruit ESP32 Huzzah Feather can be configured as a Node Controller. Warning A standalone server will have a maximum device limit of between 8-12 connected devices, due to the limitations of the Raspberry Pi's Wifi card. See Expanding the Number of Connected Devices below for how to expand this setup beyond this limit. Troubleshooting the Standalone Server: ¶ On the Aether-Local network you can access a terminal on the PI via SSH. Open a command prompt and enter ssh aether@aether the password for SSH to the Pi will be provided with the Image. To access the Aether Server logs use the command pm2 logs server To stop and start the server use: pm2 stop server and pm2 start server if the server was working well but has crashed and won't restart its possible that the database has been corrupted. You can restore to the last functional state by navigating to the server directory with: cd testbed-v4 and running: git restore . Expanding the Number of Connected Devices ¶ To expand the number of possible connected devices, a Router running in Access Point Mode, can be used to host the Aether-Local Wifi network: Follow your Router manufacturer's instructions to setup Access Point Mode, and set the router's SSID to Aether-Local its Security to WPA2 (Ensure the WPA2 Password matches the password defined in the firmware's aether_config.h file) and its IP Address to 172.23.4.2 . Connect the WAN port of your router to the Ethernet Port on the Raspberry Pi Setup the Raspberry Pi to use its Ethernet connection as a bridge via the network manager using the following command sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name PiBridge ifname eth0 ipv4.method shared Setup the IP Address of the ethernet bridge sudo nmcli connection modify PiBridge ipv4.addresses 172.23.4.1/24 Setup the DHCP range of the bridge connection sudo nmcli connection modify PiBridge ipv4.shared-dhcp-range "172.23.4.10,172.23.4.254 Note Make sure you disable the Wifi Access point that is running on the Pi. You can also use the Pi's wifi to connect to another internet enabled Wifi network to allow for remote access to the the Raspberry Pi if desired.
docs.title: Standalone Server - Raspberry Pi
